en: The Scripture on the Original Vows of the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmagupta of India during the Sui Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān was traveling through the human realm and arrived at Vaiśālī.

Residing in the country of Vairambhya beneath the tree named *Ratnagarbha*, he was accompanied by a great assembly of eight thousand bhikṣus and thirty-six thousand bodhisattvas, as well as kings, ministers, brahmins, householders, devas, nāgas, asuras, gandharvas, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and others; surrounded by this great multitude before him, he preached the Dharma.

At that time, Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, receiving the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, rose from his seat, bared one shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and facing the Bhagavān, joined his palms, bowed his body, and said:
“World-Honored One!

I only pray that you will proclaim the names of the Buddhas and the sublime great vows they originally made in the past, so that sentient beings, upon hearing them, may have their karmic obstructions eliminated, and so that they may be gathered in during the future time when the True Dharma is decaying.
At that time, the Bhagavān praised the youth Mañjuśrī, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent!”

The Greatly Compassionate Mañjuśrī, having aroused immeasurable pity, exhorted me to speak for the sake of benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to gods and humans, as well as for those sentient beings entangled by various karmic obstructions who seek their own welfare and benefit.
“Mañjuśrī! You should keep this well in mind and listen to what I say.
Then the youth Mañjuśrī, desiring to hear the Buddha’s teaching, addressed him, saying:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!
The Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī:
“To the east, beyond as many buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in ten Ganges Rivers, there is a world named Vaidūryanirbhāsa (Pure Lapis Lazuli). In that land there is a Buddha named:”
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān Bhaiṣajyaguruvaiḍūryaprabha.
“Mañjuśrī! When that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha, was formerly practicing the bodhisattva path, he made twelve great vows.
What are these twelve?
"First Great Vow:

May it be that when I attain perfect awakening to the Bodhi of the Buddhas in a future life, my own radiance shall blaze forth, illuminating immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless worlds; adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and the eighty minor characteristics, may my body be thus, and cause all sentient beings to be no different from me."
"The second great vow:

May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, my body shall be like lapis lazuli, pure within and without, free from all blemishes and impurities; its radiance vast and expansive, its majestic virtue blazing forth;
the body dwelling in perfect stability, adorned with a network of flames surpassing the sun and moon."

If there are sentient beings born in the intermediate spaces between worlds, or those among humans who are in darkness or at night and do not know their direction or location, by virtue of my light, they shall proceed wherever they wish and perform all their various activities.
"The third great vow:

May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, through boundless and limitless wisdom and skillful means, I shall cause the realms of immeasurable sentient beings to enjoy inexhaustible resources, ensuring that not a single person lacks anything."
"The fourth great vow:

May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, all sentient beings who follow heterodox paths shall be established in the path to Bodhi; and those who follow the path of the Śrāvakas or the path of the Pratyekabuddhas, may they all be established in the Mahāyāna."
"The fifth great vow:

May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, if there are sentient beings who practice the pure conduct within my Dharma—may these sentient beings, being immeasurable and boundless, all obtain unimpaired precepts and be endowed with the three groups of precepts, such that none ever break the precepts or fall into the evil realms."
"The sixth great vow:

May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, if there are sentient beings whose bodies are inferior, who lack their sense faculties, who are ugly, dull, and foolish, or who are deaf, blind, lame, or crippled, whose bodies are contorted or hunched, or who suffer from leprosy, insanity, or any other various physical ailments—upon hearing my name, may they all have their sense faculties restored and their bodies become complete and whole."
"The Seventh Great Vow:

May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, if there are sentient beings who are oppressed by various ailments, who have no protector, no refuge, and no dwelling place; who are deprived of all necessities of life and medicine; and who, lacking relatives, are poor and pitiable—if such persons hear my name, may all their ailments be eliminated and they be free from all pain and affliction, until they finally reach unsurpassed Bodhi."
“Eighth Great Vow:

May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, if there are women who, being oppressed by the hundred evils of the female form, feel weary of and detached from their female bodies and wish to cast off their female forms—upon hearing my name, may they transform their female bodies into the marks of a man, until they finally reach unsurpassed Bodhi.”
"The Ninth Great Vow:

May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, I shall cause all sentient beings to be liberated from the net of Māra; should they fall into the dense forest of various divergent views, I shall establish them all in right view and sequentially show them the gateways of the Bodhisattva practices."
"The tenth great vow:

May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, if there are sentient beings who are bound by various royal laws, flogged, imprisoned, or facing the death penalty, and who are beset by immeasurable calamities and tormented by grief and sorrow, suffering in both body and mind—may all such sentient beings, through the power of my merit, be completely liberated from all their afflictions."
"The eleven great vows:

'May it be that when I attain enlightenment in a future world, if there are sentient beings whose bodies are scorched by the fire of hunger and who commit various evil deeds for the sake of seeking food, I shall first satisfy their bodies with the most exquisite food of color, fragrance, and flavor, and subsequently establish them in ultimate peace and happiness through the flavor of the Dharma.'"
“The Twelve Great Vows:

‘May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, if there are sentient beings who are poor and lack clothing, and are tormented day and night by cold, heat, mosquitoes, and gadflies, I shall bestow upon them clothing for their use, in various colors according to their preferences; furthermore, with all kinds of precious ornaments, flower garlands, scented ointments, drums, music, and various performances—whatever implements sentient beings require—I shall cause them all to be fully satisfied.’”
"These twelve great vows were originally made in the past by that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabha, while he was practicing as a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!
All the vows of the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha, as well as the meritorious adornments of that Buddha-field, could not be fully described even at the end of an eon."

That Buddha-land is exclusively pure; there are no female forms, it is free from all desires and evils, and there is not even the sound of suffering from any of the evil realms. Its ground is made of lapis lazuli, and its cities, palaces, walls, gates, windows, halls, pavilions, pillars, beams, bracket sets, and surrounding nets are all composed of the seven treasures. Its adornments are just like those of the Land of Ultimate Bliss in the Pure Lapis Lazuli World.

“In that land there are two bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, one named Sūryaprabha and the other named Candraprabha, who are the foremost among the immeasurable and incalculable assembly of bodhisattvas and who uphold the treasury of the True Dharma of that World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabha.”
"Therefore, Mañjuśrī! Sons and daughters of good family who possess faith should aspire to be born in that Buddha-field.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the youth Mañjuśrī, saying:

“Mañjuśrī! There may be sentient beings who do not distinguish between good and evil, who are full of greed and never satisfied, who do not understand generosity or the karmic fruits of giving, who are foolish and lacking in wisdom, deficient in the faculty of faith, and who amass wealth only to guard it jealously, unwilling to share or give it away.”
Because these sentient beings lack a mind of generosity, when they see a beggar approach, their hearts are not gladdened; it is as if their own flesh were being cut away.

Furthermore, there are immeasurable sentient beings who are stingy and greedy; they do not enjoy things themselves, nor do they wish to give them to their parents or wives and children, much less to their slaves, servants, or other beggars.
These sentient beings, having ended their lives in the human realm, are reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts or the realm of animals.

Because they previously heard the name of that Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha while in the human realm, the name of the Tathāgata briefly appears before them while they are in the realm of ghosts or animals. At the very moment of this recollection, they die there and are reborn again in the human realm. They attain the knowledge of past lives, fear the miserable destinies, take no pleasure in sensual desires, delight in practicing wise giving, praise those who give, and are able to relinquish all they possess. Gradually, they give even their head, eyes, hands, feet, blood, flesh, and limbs to those who ask, let alone other material wealth.
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!
There are sentient beings who, although they have received from the Tathāgata and uphold the precepts for training, nevertheless violate the precepts, violate their conduct, and violate right view;
or, while receiving the precepts for training and guarding the prohibitions, they do not seek extensive learning and do not understand the profound meaning within the sūtras spoken by the Tathāgata."

Or again, there may be those who, though possessing great learning, harbor overweening pride, asserting themselves to be right while disparaging others; they revile and slander the true Dharma and become partisans of Māra.
Such deluded persons, as well as other immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of sentient beings who follow false paths, shall fall into hell.

These sentient beings, who would otherwise have wandered through the hells for an indefinite period, because they have heard the name of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha, will—through the power of that Buddha and the manifestation of the Tathāgata’s name before them while in the hellish realm—immediately cast off their lives and be reborn in the human realm. Possessing right view and diligence, with a pure and virtuous mind, they will then renounce the household life, go forth into homelessness within the teaching of the Tathāgata to study the Path, and gradually practice all the bodhisattva deeds.
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!
There may be sentient beings who, out of jealousy, praise only themselves and do not praise others.
Because these beings exalt themselves and disparage others, they will undergo various bitter sufferings in the three evil realms for immeasurable thousands of years."

After passing through immeasurable thousands of years, they die there and are reborn in the realm of animals, becoming oxen, horses, camels, or donkeys; tormented by hunger and thirst, beaten with whips and sticks, and burdened with heavy loads, they travel along the roads.
If they are reborn in the human realm, they always dwell in lowly and base conditions, becoming slaves or servants to others, subject to their驱使 (driving and service).

If, in a previous human life, one has heard the name of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha, by virtue of these roots of goodness, they shall be liberated from all sufferings; their faculties will become sharp and keen, and they will possess wisdom and broad learning. They will constantly seek the source of all that is good, always follow and associate with virtuous friends, and be able to sever the snares of Māra, break the shell of ignorance, dry up the river of afflictions, and be liberated from all birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, pain, and distress.
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī! There are sentient beings who delight in causing estrangement and engage in mutual strife and litigation.

These beings, who harbor malicious intentions toward one another, constantly commit various evils through body, speech, and mind. Desiring to harm each other, they constantly inflict useless injuries upon one another. They may report their grievances to forest deities, tree deities, mountain deities, cemetery deities, and various other distinct spirits; they slaughter domestic animals and take their flesh and blood to sacrifice to all the yakṣas and rākṣasas who consume flesh and blood. They write the names of their enemies and fashion their likenesses, performing various poisonous harms, incantations, sorcery, demonic arts, and corpse-raising spells, desiring to cut off the lives of others and destroy their bodies."

By virtue of hearing the name of the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha, these various evils shall be unable to cause harm; instead, they will all give rise to thoughts of mutual loving-kindness, beneficial intent, and freedom from resentment, each rejoicing and mutually supporting one another.
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!

These fourfold assemblies—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—as well as other sons and daughters of good family endowed with faith, who observe the eightfold fast for one year or for three months and uphold the various precepts, shall, by virtue of these roots of goodness, according to their inclinations and their aspirations, if they wish to be reborn in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss in the presence of the Tathāgata Amitābha, be able to do so because they have heard the name of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha. At the time of their death, eight bodhisattvas will descend from the sky to show them the path, and they will be spontaneously born within various multicolored padma lotuses in that realm.

Furthermore, if this person desires to be reborn in the heavens, they shall immediately attain rebirth there; their original roots of goodness from the past will be inexhaustible, and they shall no longer be born in any other miserable realms. When their life in the heavens ends, they shall be born among humans as a Wheel-Turning King, exercising sovereignty over the four continents and establishing immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of sentient beings in the ten paths of wholesome action. Alternatively, they may be born into a great kṣatriya clan, a great brāhmaṇa clan, or a great householder family, with stores of gold, silver, grain, and silk filling their granaries and treasuries; they will be endowed with perfect physical form, perfect sovereignty, and perfect retinues, being courageous, robust, and powerful like a great athlete.
If there is a woman who hears the proclamation of this Tathāgata’s name and receives and upholds it with a sincere heart, she shall forever be freed from the female body hereafter.
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

In the future, by means of various skillful methods, I shall cause the name of that World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha, to be circulated and heard among faithful sons and daughters of good family; I shall even awaken their ears to the Buddha’s name during their sleep.”

If one upholds this sutra, recites it, and proclaims it; or if one explains and analyzes it for others; or if one writes it oneself, or causes another to write it; or if one takes a scroll of the sutra and wraps it in five-colored pure cloth, sweeps and cleans a pure place to install it there, and makes offerings with various flowers, various incenses, unguents, garlands, jeweled banners, and canopies—then at that time, the Four Great Heavenly Kings, together with their retinues and hundreds of thousands of koṭis and nayutas of other devas, will all go to that place.

Wherever this sutra scroll circulates, or wherever there may be someone who recites and upholds it, because they have heard the name of that World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha, and because of his excellent and great vows made in the past, you should know that in such places there shall be no further untimely deaths; nor shall beings be possessed by various ghosts who seize their souls and spirits. Even if they have already been seized, they shall be restored to their former state.
The Buddha said: "So it is, so it is! Mañjuśrī!"
It is as you have said,
Mañjuśrī! If a son or daughter of good family with faith wishes to make offerings to that Tathāgata, they should...
A person should fashion an image of the Tathāgata, observe the eightfold fast for seven days and seven nights while consuming pure food,
scatter various flowers in a clean place, burn various incenses, and adorn that location with various silken fabrics,
banners, and streamers; having bathed and purified themselves, they should put on new, clean garments.
One should give rise to a mind free from defilement and turbidity, a mind free from anger and malice, and toward all sentient beings, a mind of benefit,
as well as a mind of equanimity characterized by loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and impartiality. One should play music, sing praises,
and circumambulate the Buddha image to the right, while recollecting the great original vows of that Tathāgata and explaining this sutra, just as one has contemplated.
Through mindfulness, whatever one aspires for and all that one desires shall be perfectly fulfilled:
those who seek long life obtain long life; those who seek merit and reward obtain merit and reward; those who seek mastery obtain mastery;
and those who seek sons or daughters obtain sons or daughters.

Furthermore, if there are those who suddenly experience bad dreams, see various evil omens, or witness strange birds gathering, such that a hundred anomalies appear at their dwelling, if these people can honor and make offerings to that Bhaisajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabhā Tathāgata with various requisites, all evil dreams, evil omens, and inauspicious events will entirely vanish. Or, if they face fears of water, fire, weapons, poison, or precipices; or fears of wild elephants, lions, tigers, wolves, bears, brown bears, venomous snakes, malignant scorpions, centipedes, and millipedes—if they mindfully recall and make offerings to that Tathāgata, they shall be liberated from all such fears.
If there are threats such as foreign invasions, banditry, or rebellions, one should likewise call that Tathāgata to mind with reverence and respect.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!

If there are faithful sons or daughters of good family who, for as long as they live, take the three refuges and do not serve other deities; or who observe the five precepts, or the ten precepts, or the one hundred and four precepts of a bodhisattva, or further leave the household life to observe the two hundred and fifty precepts of a bhikṣu, or the five hundred precepts of a bhikṣuṇī—if, within the midst of these various observances, they should violate any of the prohibitive precepts and fear falling into the evil realms, yet are able to make offerings to that World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabha, they will certainly not undergo retribution in the three evil realms.

If there are women who, when on the verge of giving birth, undergo extreme suffering, should they be able to invoke the name and make offerings to that World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru Vaidūryaprabha, they will quickly attain liberation; the child they bear shall have complete physical faculties, a handsome appearance that brings joy to all who see it, sharp and intelligent faculties, peace and security with little illness, and no non-human spirits shall seize their soul or spirit.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying: “Ānanda,
do you believe and accept all the merits of that World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha, as I have extolled them?”
"You have given rise to much doubt regarding such profound spheres of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O Great Virtuous World-Honored One!"
Regarding the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata, I no longer have any doubt.
Why is this? Because there is nothing—whether in the conduct of body, speech, or mind—that is not pure in all Tathāgatas.
World-Honored One!

These sun and moon possess such great supernormal powers and such great majesty that they could be made to fall; even Sumeru, the king of mountains, could be moved. Yet, there is no discrepancy whatsoever in what the Buddhas have spoken.
"O Great Virtuous World-Honored One!
There may be sentient beings who lack the faculty of faith; having heard the teaching on the Buddha-realm of the Tathāgata, they might think:
'How can one obtain such vast merit merely by recollecting the name of that Tathāgata?'"

"If they do not believe or accept this in their hearts, but instead give rise to slander, these people will for a long night experience no meaningful benefit and shall fall into the realms of suffering.
The Buddha said, "Ānanda!"
If the name of that Tathāgata should enter one’s ears, it is impossible for such a person to fall into the evil realms.

Ānanda! The realm of the Buddhas is truly difficult to believe; that you now have faith and accept it should be known as entirely due to the majestic power of the Tathāgata. It is not something that can be believed or accepted by any Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha, with the sole exception of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who are in their last birth before Buddhahood (Ekajātipratibaddha).
Ānanda! A human body is difficult to obtain; it is also difficult to find faith, reverence, and respect for the Triple Gem; but to hear the name of that Tathāgata is even more difficult than this.

Ānanda! Regarding the immeasurable bodhisattva practices, the immeasurable skillful means, and the immeasurable vast vows of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha—if I were to explain those vows and practices of that Tathāgata for an eon, or even more than an eon, until the very end of the eon, I would still not have exhausted the account of the former deeds and the sublime great vows performed by that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha.

At that time, there was among the assembly a bodhisattva-mahāsattva named Jue-tuo (Trāṇamukta). He rose from his seat, bared one shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and, facing the Bhagavān with palms joined and body bowed, addressed him, saying:
“Virtuous World-Honored One!

In future ages, there will be sentient beings whose bodies are afflicted by grave illnesses; long suffering from emaciation, they will be unable to eat, tormented by hunger and thirst, their throats and lips parched, and the signs of death will manifest before them. Their vision will fail, and they will be surrounded by weeping parents, kinsmen, friends, and acquaintances. While the person’s corpse lies in its place, the messengers of Yama will lead their consciousness before Yama, the Dharma King. Behind this person stands the co-nascent deity (*sahaja-devatā*), who records everything they have done—whether sin or merit—and delivers this entire record to Yama, the Dharma King.
At that time, King Yama, the Dharma King, will interrogate that person, calculate their deeds, and pass judgment according to their good or evil.
If they can take refuge in that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha, and make offerings to him according to the Dharma, they shall immediately be restored to health.

When this person’s consciousness returns, they will remember everything as if awakening from a dream. Whether it be after seven days, twenty-one days, thirty-five days, or forty-nine days, once the consciousness has returned, they will fully recall all their karmic retributions for good and evil deeds; because they have realized this for themselves, they will not commit further evil acts even at the cost of their lives.
"Therefore, sons and daughters of good family who possess faith should make offerings to the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda asked the Bodhisattva Trāṇamukta:
"O son of good family!"
"How should one make offerings to that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabha?
The Bodhisattva Trāṇamukta replied,
"Venerable Ānanda!..."

If there is a person suffering from illness who wishes to be liberated from a grave malady, one should observe the eightfold fast for this person for seven days and seven nights. One should provide food, drink, and various requisites according to one's means to make offerings to the community of bhikṣus. Day and night, during the six periods, one should prostrate and make offerings to that World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha. One should recite this sutra forty-nine times, light forty-nine lamps, and fashion seven images of that Tathāgata. Before each image, place seven lamps; each lamp should be as large as a chariot wheel, or alternatively, their light should remain unextinguished for up to forty-nine days. Furthermore, one should fashion five-colored silk banners forty-nine feet in length.
"Furthermore, Venerable Ānanda!

When calamities arise for consecrated Kṣatriya kings—namely, the calamity of pestilence among the people, the calamity of invasion by foreign powers, the calamity of internal rebellion within their own realm, the calamity of portents in the stars and constellations, the calamity of eclipses of the sun and moon, the calamity of unseasonable winds and rains, or the calamity of drought when the time for rain has passed—at that time, these consecrated Kṣatriya kings should give rise to a heart of compassion toward all sentient beings, release those who are imprisoned, and, according to the previously described ritual methods of offering, make offerings to that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha."

At that time, by means of these roots of goodness, and through the power of the former supreme vows of the World-Honored One, the Medicine Master Lapis Lazuli Light Tathāgata, the realm of that consecrated Kṣatriya king shall immediately attain peace and security. Wind and rain will fall in their proper seasons, the crops will flourish, and the land will be bountiful. All sentient beings within the kingdom will be free from illness and live in peace and happiness, giving rise to much joy. Furthermore, within that kingdom, there will be no disturbances caused by yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, or other malevolent spirits. All evil omens will cease to appear, and the life span, physical vigor, freedom from disease, and sovereignty of that consecrated Kṣatriya king will all be increased.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda asked the Bodhisattva Rescuer and Deliverer:
"Good son, how can a life that has already reached its end be further extended?"
The Bodhisattva Trāṇamukta said,
“Ānanda! Have you not heard what the Tathāgata has taught regarding the nine types of untimely death?”
Therefore, they are instructed in the expedient means of mantras and medicines;

or there may be sentient beings whose illness is not grave, yet they lack medicine or a caregiver, or perhaps a physician treats them incorrectly, causing them to die prematurely—this is the first untimely death.
The second untimely death is being executed by the laws of the state.
The third untimely death is when one who hunts, is dissolute, or is intoxicated by lust beyond measure has their soul and spirit harmed by non-human beings;
the fourth untimely death is being burned by fire;
the fifth untimely death is being drowned by water.
The sixth untimely death is entering among lions, tigers, leopards, and various other evil beasts.
The seventh untimely death is being tormented by hunger and thirst, unable to obtain food or drink, and thereby meeting one's end.
The eighth untimely death is being harmed by malevolent incantations, poisons, and reanimated corpses.

The ninth untimely death is to throw oneself from a cliff to seek death. This is what the Tathāgata has briefly described as the nine kinds of great untimely deaths; furthermore, there are immeasurable other forms of untimely death.
At that time, there were twelve yakṣa generals present among the assembly, seated together in the gathering.
They were as follows: General Piṅgala, General Vajra, General Mekhala, and General Anala.
The Great General Antara, the Great General Manera,
the Great General Indra, the Great General Pāyila,
the Great General Mahura, and the Great General Cindala.
The Great General Cāṇūra and the Great General Piṅgala—
these twelve yakṣa generals, each with a retinue of seven thousand yakṣas, all spoke with one voice to the World-Honored One, saying:

"Having now received the power of the Buddha’s majesty and having heard the name of the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha, we shall no longer have any fear of the evil realms."

We now all share one mind; until the end of our lives, we take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṃgha. We shall all bear the burden of all sentient beings, acting for their benefit, welfare, and peace and happiness. In whatever village, city, town, or forest hermitage this sutra may be circulated, or wherever there are those who uphold the name of the World-Honored One, Bhaisajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha Tathāgata, and draw near to him with offerings—we, his retinue, will protect such persons, causing them all to be liberated from every suffering and difficulty, and ensuring that all their requests are fully satisfied.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the yakṣa generals, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
Great yakṣa generals!"
"If you all would keep in mind the grace and virtue of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha, you should keep in mind the benefit of all sentient beings.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"What is the name of this sutra?
How should it be upheld?
The Buddha said:
“Ānanda! This Dharma gate is named ‘The Supreme Great Vows Originally Made by the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha’; you should uphold it as such.
It is also named ‘The Self-Vow of the Twelve Great Yakṣa Generals’; you should uphold it as such.”
"It is named 'The Purification of All Karmic Obstructions'; you should uphold it thus.

When the Bhagavān had finished speaking these words, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, the great śrāvakas, kings, ministers, brahmins, householders, and the entire assembly—including asuras, gandharvas, and others—having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Scripture on the Original Vows of the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru Spoken by the Buddha.
